UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                     BEFORE THE
                       FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION


                                                              )
 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.                                  )            Docket No. ER26-3380-000
                                                              )

                                      COMMENTS OF GOOGLE LLC

          Pursuant to Rule 211 of the Rules of Practice and Procedure of the Federal Energy

Regulatory Commission (“Commission”),1 Google LLC (“Google”) hereby submits these

comments regarding PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.’s (“PJM”) Reliability Backstop Procurement

(“RBP”) Proposal. Google commends PJM for taking steps to ensure reliability, which must

remain its first priority. Nevertheless, while RBP may help maintain near-term resource adequacy,

Google urges PJM to focus future efforts on reforms that incentivize new large loads to procure

and bring their own new generation rather than relying on an interim, one-time solicitation, like

RBP. As explained below, Google believes that this bilateral contracting will do more to procure

the necessary supply—after all, there is no guarantee that RBP will procure enough GW to cover

the shortfall2—and do so in a way that meets future demand on a durable, forward-looking basis,

rather than relying on measures that address only previously identified reliability needs. A bilateral

approach also does more to ensure the new supply meets the needs and preferences of new large

load customers, unlocking the economic growth benefits that they can provide. And it’s not just

       Google that sees the promise of new large loads bilaterally contracting for new generation. During

      the RBP stakeholder process, in response to a Request for Information released by PJM, a

      “[m]ajority of parties expressed interest and preference to a bilateral contract over a central

      procurement.”3 Respondents to the Request for Information spanned the large load, supply, and

      utilities sectors.4

 I.       WHO WE ARE

              Google’s mission is to organize the world’s information and make it universally accessible

      and useful. AI is critical to that mission. Data centers necessary to serve Google’s customers

      consume a large amount of electricity and require reliable electric service to operate. As Google’s

      business grows, so too does its demand for reliable, affordable, and clean electricity.

II.       COMMENTS

              Google recognizes that the unprecedented load growth that PJM is currently experiencing

      is both a tremendous opportunity and a complex challenge. The load growth reflects the

      dynamism of the nation’s technology sector, which can drive economic growth, create jobs, and

      significantly expand the tax base of the areas in which that growth occurs. Those are real,

      verifiable benefits that accrue across the local, state, and national levels, and should be available

      to the communities that want to host the necessary digital and energy infrastructure.

              But those economic benefits must not come at the cost of sacrificing the reliability and

      affordability to which customers in those communities, and PJM more broadly, are rightly

      accustomed. RBP may help protect against that result in the short term by procuring additional

                                                             -2-
 generation to ensure reliability and allocating the costs of that additional generation to the

entities that caused the need for it, namely the new large loads that have not secured sufficient

capacity to offset their demand. Anything else would be unjust and unreasonable and manifestly

contrary to the principles that Google has consistently supported through its Capacity

Commitment Framework (“CCF”), as well as the White House’s Ratepayer Protection Pledge

and the Statement of Principles from the National Energy Dominance Council and the PJM

Governors.5 But the Commission alone cannot ensure that result, as PJM itself acknowledged in

a letter to the region’s governors in May. The retail level is where the rubber meets the road.

Indeed, as PJM stated, “if states have not established frameworks to appropriately allocate costs

to new data center loads, it is unclear to which customers those costs would be assigned,” and “it

appears possible to PJM that these costs will be allocated to other consumers.”6 To date, not all

PJM states have taken comprehensive steps to establish and implement these contemplated

frameworks across PJM’s diverse footprint. If RBP is accepted, the states must take up the

mantle and ensure that the costs of RBP are allocated in a manner that is just and reasonable and

consistent with the Ratepayer Protection Pledge. Google stands ready to engage in that process

to achieve that result.

        And while RBP may be a reasonable response to PJM’s current circumstances, a more

permanent, long-term framework is necessary. Constantly shifting, unpredictable regulatory

constructs undermine the investor confidence necessary to support the multi-billion-dollar

investments in new capacity needed to ensure reliability and affordability over the long term.

                                                         -3-
 That is particularly true for regulatory changes that call into question or cast doubt upon

contracts, such as firm electric service agreements or bilateral contracts between generation and

load, which were entered into in reliance on the rules in effect at the time of execution. Rather

than accepting constant change and uncertainty, the Commission, PJM, and all stakeholders

should focus on developing the stable, predictable investment conditions that will facilitate the

investments needed to extricate PJM from its present resource adequacy shortfall and maintain

resource adequacy in the long-term.

        Finally, Google also believes strongly that new capacity requires corresponding

investments in the transmission infrastructure necessary to ensure that that capacity can be

interconnected promptly and used to serve load reliably. Google has been transparent with

utility partners about its plans for demand growth across PJM for years, including by signing

long-term contracts with utilities that provide clear growth projections and associated ramp rates.

Yet the development of the energy infrastructure needed to accommodate that load growth and

the corresponding new capacity needed to protect other ratepayers has lagged badly behind.

While Google is prepared to bear the costs appropriately attributable to its growth, Google is not

in a position to develop that transmission infrastructure unilaterally. Accordingly, Google urges

PJM not to lose sight of the need to proactively develop the transmission infrastructure that is

critical to maintaining reliability and affordability.

        1. A Viable Long-Term Solution to PJM’s Capacity Shortfall is a Bring Your Own
           New Capacity Framework that Protects Existing Ratepayers from Cost Shifts and
           Stranded Asset Risk

        Google has long advocated for the principle that new large loads should pay for the costs

associated with the increase in demand that they are driving and the strain that puts on existing




                                                         -4-
 infrastructure. The CCF that Google has advocated for at the state level7 and the “Bring Your

Own New Capacity” (“BYONC”) framework that Google has advocated for at the federal level

both reflect that principle.

          At the federal level, Google has consistently argued that new large loads must bring their

own new generation to support the demands they place on existing electrical infrastructure,

where existing structures, like the Reliability Pricing Model (“RPM”), have not secured adequate

new supply.8 Although not a silver bullet, requiring new large loads that interconnect to the grid

to secure their own capacity is the single most important mechanism for shielding existing

customers from adverse rate impacts of those new large loads. Indeed, from the outset of PJM’s

first Critical Issue Fast Path (“CIFP”) focused on large load issues, Google has supported this

concept, including through a BYONC framework with an accelerated pathway for new

generation and new load to interconnect to the transmission system.9

          BYONC is the centerpiece of Google’s own procurement philosophy. Google strives to

serve every new MW of data center load with a new MW of capacity in the same balancing

authority, ensuring that its new large loads do not draw down on the reserve margin financed by

existing customers.10 This approach enables Google to choose the right size and mix of capacity

assets to meet its needs, which can include demand-side resources that PJM’s existing rules do

 not accommodate.11 Google’s agreements with Voltus to unlock up to 100 MW of capacity from

distributed energy resources in PJM12 and with Indiana Michigan Power (I&M) to leverage

demand response to reduce I&M’s peak load13 are examples of the type of innovative solutions

to the capacity shortfall that BYONC enables. In addition, as a customer-driven approach,

BYONC allows Google and other data center developers to invest in capacity solutions that can

scale to meet projected growth, which provides a forward-looking and more durable means to

protect customers from the demand-driven effects of new large loads than backward-looking

measures like RBP. In short, a BYONC framework can unlock more capacity and do so in

advance of the identified reliability needs—a result that is better for all PJM customers.

         The BYONC framework is also consistent with the White House’s Ratepayer Protection

Pledge, under which companies including Google have committed to build, bring, or buy the

new generation and electricity needed to meet their new demand and to pay for it whether or not

they ultimately use it, and the Statement of Principles from the National Energy Dominance

Council and the PJM Governors.14

         On the state level, Google’s CCF is built on five key pillars that complement a BYONC

approach:

capacity from participating in the market. Given the shortfall PJM faces, it should accommodate any and all MWs that
a capacity resource or market participant can physically supply.

    1. Non-Discriminatory Applicability: Terms should apply to all new large
      loads with an expected peak demand above a certain threshold. Regulators
      should avoid adoption of mandatory terms for specific end uses of
      electricity.
   2. Long-Term Commitment: New large loads should be required to sign a
      long-term contract that ensures that the customer commits to providing
      sufficient revenue to cover the investments made on their behalf.
      Regulators should consider flexibility for customers to ramp into their load
      over time.
   3. Significant Minimum Charges: New large loads should be required to pay
      costs of power capacity (e.g., approximated via demand charges) at a
      sufficient minimum to guard against potential cost shifting in the event that
      metered customer demand is significantly lower than planned for.
   4. Upfront Collateral: To ensure financial stability of the requesting customer,
      regulators should consider the appropriate role for upfront collateral to
      provide financial assurance to the utility that the long-term contract
      minimums can be met.
   5. Flexible and Transparent Fees for Modifications: To protect other
      ratepayers, while also maintaining reasonable flexibility for new large
      loads, regulators should consider appropriate notice periods and fees for
      contract cancellation or capacity reduction.


         Google has worked with industry stakeholders to refine retail tariffs so that they

incorporate and/or reflect the protections and principles of the CCF. For example, Google

collaborated with stakeholders representing diverse interests, including I&M, the Indiana Office

of Utility Consumer Counselor, the Citizens Action Coalition, the Data Center Coalition, and

other large load customers to reform I&M’s Industrial Power Tariff to protect existing retail

customers from stranded asset risks. The resulting tariff, which applies to 70-MW large loads at

a single site, includes a 12-year minimum contract term, an 80 percent minimum monthly billing

demand tied to the customer’s contract capacity, and exit fees.15 Google helped secure a




   15

                                                           -7-
 unanimous settlement,16 which illustrates that consumer protection and energy infrastructure

development need not be at odds. As of July 2026, the CCF has been adopted by 12 utilities in

11 states.

          2. The Costs of the RBP Must Be Allocated in a Manner that Complies with Cost
             Causation, the CCF, the Ratepayer Protection Pledge, and the Statement of
             Principles from the NEDC and the PJM Governors

          As noted above, Google recognizes that RBP may be a reasonable response to the current

resource adequacy shortfall, but it should not become a permanent substitute for market-driven,

long-term mechanisms that deliver resource adequacy at just and reasonable rates. Indeed, Google

is concerned that, as things stand, RBP could lead to the sort of cost shifting that Google has long

advocated against and that would be inconsistent with both the Ratepayer Protection Pledge and

the National Energy Dominance Council and PJM Governors’ Statement of Principles.17 Because

not all states in PJM have separate mechanisms for allocating costs directly to large loads, there is

no way to ensure that the costs of RBP can be allocated exclusively to those that have not already

covered their load. It should be incumbent on PJM to proactively coordinate with states to ensure

that they have the retail mechanisms in place to properly allocate to new large loads the costs that

RBP would impose.

          To that end, Google applauds and supports the collaborative effort announced by the

Virginia State Corporation Commission (“VA SCC”) and the Data Center Coalition (“DCC”) to

develop model state tariff provisions addressing the retail allocation of RBP costs, among other

necessary criteria (e.g., geographic matching of load and supply). Such provisions are designed

to assign RBP costs to the large load customers whose demand causes the need for those

 procurements. That is a necessary step to protect residential and existing commercial and

industrial customers from cost shifts.18 Google is committed to participating in that effort and

doing everything it reasonably can to help ensure adequate protections are in place, building on

our proven track record of advancing responsible grid solutions. In addition, given the importance

of those efforts and the States’ exclusive authority over the retail cost allocation mechanisms,

Google urges PJM to be prepared to accommodate the needs of the States, ensuring that they have

the information that they need and the costs are allocated on timelines that consider and reflect

state retail ratemaking processes.

          3. PJM Must Make Progress to Address the Additional Factors Contributing to the
             Current Resource Adequacy Shortfall

          Reforms that require new large loads to secure their own new capacity are a critical element

of ensuring reliability and affordability. Yet they are only part of the answer. As Google has

consistently maintained, one of the chief barriers to the integration of new large loads in a manner

that does not undermine affordability and reliability are long interconnection timelines and the

“[t]erawatts of new generation capacity [that] are stuck in interconnection queues because

inadequate transmission infrastructure” renders interconnection too slow, too expensive, or both.19

New large loads cannot bring forth new capacity resources if those resources’ interconnection to

the transmission system is stymied or delayed due to unpredictable—and often high—network

upgrade costs or delays in identifying or developing that infrastructure.

             Further, PJM’s existing rules also unnecessarily limit the ability of new storage resources

to use Surplus Interconnection Service (“SIS”) to provide additional capacity, even where Capacity

Interconnection Rights (“CIRs”) at the same point of interconnection are underutilized. Where

storage is added to an existing inverter-based resource, PJM requires the resources to operate as a

single hybrid resource for the storage to access those CIRs, which can significantly limit the

commercial viability of the arrangement.20 And where storage is added to a non-inverter-based

resource, such as a gas generator, PJM’s mixed-technology facility rules do not permit the storage

resource to use those CIRs to increase the facility’s unforced capacity (“UCAP”) contribution at

all.

            These barriers could be addressed through a relatively straightforward rule change allowing

an existing resource with underutilized CIRs to allocate a portion of those rights to a new resource

interconnecting through SIS. Because the surplus resource must be studied before receiving SIS,

PJM can identify and impose any necessary restrictions through that process to address reliability,

operational, or market-power concerns. Such a reform could unlock significant amounts of

additional capacity from storage using existing interconnection capability and allow that capacity

to come online more quickly.

            Google intends to work with PJM and its stakeholders to address these barriers promptly.

Google is not asking the Commission to resolve these issues in this proceeding but respectfully

requests that the Commission encourage PJM to pursue reforms that make more efficient use of

existing interconnection capability as part of its ongoing efforts to address the region’s resource

        adequacy challenges. If these barriers cannot be addressed expeditiously through the stakeholder

       process, further Commission attention may be warranted.

              Although Google recognizes the significant progress that PJM has made and continues to

       pursue on interconnection reform, these issues remain a major reason why, at the moment, supply

       is not keeping up with demand. Resolving that imbalance also requires coordinated, holistic

       transmission planning processes that reflect the growing demands placed on the grid by both new

       demand and new supply. Given the scale, pace, and volume of large load interconnection requests

       as well as the corresponding scale, pace, and volume of new generator interconnection requests—

       both of which contribute significantly to the need for new transmission infrastructure—

       transmission planners must have a realistic picture of the generators and large loads planning to

       interconnect to the transmission grid so that they can develop the transmission system that

       accommodates both sides of the supply and demand equation. Only then will PJM have the

       infrastructure foundation needed to maintain resource adequacy at just and reasonable rates and

       capitalize on the economic opportunity that load growth presents without succumbing to its

       challenges.

III.      CONCLUSION

              PJM is right to focus on ensuring reliability and affordability. However, a more enduring

       structural approach is preferable to perpetual reliance on RBP or similar stopgap mechanisms.

       BYONC frameworks can unlock more capacity, do so in advance of the relevant reliability needs,

       and automatically ensure that the costs of new demand are borne by the entities that cause those

       costs. That is a much better result for PJM and all its stakeholders. Accordingly, BYONC should

       form the foundation for future PJM and Commission efforts to address the demand-driven effects

       of new large loads.
